question: Tell me about a time you changed a plan because of something you learned about the customer. What did the change cost?

raiseTranscript.text: Tell me about a time you changed a plan because of something you learned about the customer. What did the change cost?

I was building a dashboard for internal users and had planned a set of filters based on what the PM asked for. During a quick user test with two analysts I learned they needed date-range presets instead because they ran the same reports weekly. I swapped the filter UI in the last sprint.
What did that swap actually cost?
It pushed back the release by two days and I had to drop one nice-to-have chart. My manager was fine with it once I showed the test notes.
How did you know the change actually helped?
The two analysts said it saved them time in the follow-up chat and the PM logged fewer support questions after launch.

junior.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar on Wow the Customer for a junior. The candidate identified a concrete customer friction during their own work, adjusted scope, and accepted a small delivery cost without escalation. The story stays local to one feature yet shows clear ownership of the outcome. Quote about analysts confirming time savings ties the change directly to customer value. Biggest strength is willingness to trade a chart for usability instead of defending the original plan.

raiseTranscript.text: Tell me about a time you changed a plan because of something you learned about the customer. What did the change cost?

Our team was building a self-service reporting tool for three partner teams. After shadowing two power users I realized they needed bulk export before the fancy viz builder we had prioritized. I convinced the other two teams to deprioritize their custom viz requests so we could ship exports first.
What did that shift actually cost?
We delayed two partner integrations by six weeks and one team had to keep using manual reports longer. I tracked the extra support tickets during that period and it was about 12 per week.
How did you get the other teams to agree?
I showed the usage data from the shadow sessions and offered to help them with a workaround until the viz work resumed.

raiseTranscript.text: Tell me about a time you changed a plan because of something you learned about the customer. What did the change cost?

We were six months into a platform migration that would consolidate three legacy products. Customer interviews in month four showed that mid-market buyers valued integration with their existing stack far more than the unified UI we had promised the board. I recommended we pause the migration and instead build a lightweight integration layer on top of the legacy systems.
What did pausing the migration cost?

We wrote off roughly four million in sunk migration work, delayed the org-wide cost savings target by nine months, and had to reset expectations with the board. In exchange we kept 80 percent of the mid-market revenue that was at risk.
How did you handle the board conversation?
I brought the raw interview clips and revenue-at-risk model so the discussion stayed on customer retention rather than internal optics.

Biggest strength is willingness to absorb org-level cost to retain mid-market revenue instead of defending the original plan.
